solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Thing that vexes drivers aplenty, for instance?

indicators.note: for instance says the word before it is an example of the wordplay, so the clue is read in reverse from result to instruction

parts.note: the word aplenty is an example of the letters of a motoring fine rearranged, so the clue word illustrates the phrase read cryptically

explanation.surface: A grumble that motorists are vexed by plenty of things.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'fixed' as 'rearranged': the word APLENTY is PENALTY with its letters fixed into a new order, so 'aplenty' is an instance of the answer read cryptically.
explanation.definitionFit: A set fine issued on the spot for a traffic offence is something that annoys motorists.

clue.text: Conclude note with a line that's outrageous

parts.note: to conclude is to infer

explanation.surface: Ending a letter with a remark that turns out to be scandalous.
explanation.definitionFit: Infernal is used informally for something outrageous or detestable, as in 'an infernal racket'.

clue.text: Divine chap's in capsized tender

indicators.note: a boat that has capsized is upside down, so in this down clue the word is turned the other way

parts.note: tender means sore, as a bruise is

explanation.surface: A godly man is found in an overturned ship's boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' suggests a small boat to go with 'capsized', but it means painful.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of love is a deity, a divine male figure.

clue.text: With girls in peril trembling, Earl's able to seize …

indicators.note: the girls are placed in the jumbled word, so one piece goes inside the other
something trembling is shaken about, so the letters of peril are jumbled

parts.note: hens is slang for girls or women, as in a hen party

explanation.surface: Girls in danger and shaking while a nobleman can grab hold of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'girls' as hens is informal, as in a hen party; 'trembling' jumbles the word peril before the girls go into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehensile tail or limb is one capable of grasping things, such as a monkey's tail.

clue.text: … dope from container upended over Joker

indicators.note: something upended is turned upside down, so in this down clue the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a tin is a container
a wit is a joker, someone who makes funny remarks

explanation.surface: Drugs come out of an overturned box above a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' looks like drugs, linking to the previous clue's ellipsis, but means a fool. 'upended' makes NIT from TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal names for a stupid person, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Original outfit stretched out on sofa with no sides

parts.note: lay is the past tense of lie, so 'lay' means was stretched out

indicators.note: losing its sides means the word for sofa has its first and last letters removed

parts.note: a settee is a sofa

explanation.surface: Someone lounging on a sofa with no arms in their first set of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no sides' cuts SETTEE down to ETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete set of clothes and linen for a newborn baby is the first wardrobe a person ever has.

clue.text: Not at all comely, our Wee Free

indicators.note: free means loose, so the letters of these words are set loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: A dig that members of a strict Scottish church are not attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wee Free is the nickname of the Free Church of Scotland; here 'Free' is just the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are polite replies to thanks, conveying that no gratitude is needed.

clue.text: Occupy oneself dubiously and scram

definitions.meaning: to be busy at some mischief or illicit activity
slang order to go away at once

explanation.surface: Keeping busy with something shady and then running off.
explanation.definitionFit: One phrase read literally means to be engaged in something; as a command it is slang for clearing off.

clue.text: Steak or grouse?

explanation.definitionFit: The word means cow meat and, informally, a grievance or complaint.

clue.text: Your turn to have a bowl?

definitions.text: Your turn to have a bowl?

parts.words: Your turn to have a bowl?
parts.note: in cricket a set of six balls is bowled by one player, so handing someone the ball for their set is giving them the next one

explanation.surface: Passing someone the dish or invitation to take their go.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an over is a set of six balls delivered by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase hands the next go to someone, and literally assigns them the next six-ball set in cricket.

clue.text: Appearance of justice? No — fobbed off without foundation

indicators.note: something gone off is spoiled or out of order, so these letters are rearranged
without means lacking, so a word for foundation is taken out

parts.note: a bed is a foundation, as in a bed of concrete

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that apparent fairness was refused and they were fobbed off with no basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes BED from FOBBED to leave FOB; 'off' then rearranges JUSTICE, NO and FOB.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from the look of a sailing ship's foresail, refers to a person's general look or manner.

clue.text: Somewhat in rut, put back revival

indicators.note: put back means the letters are read from right to left
somewhat means only part of these words is taken

explanation.surface: Something stuck in a rut gets returned and then makes a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' takes part of 'in rut, put' and 'back' reads it right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: An improvement or recovery in fortunes, as in a market, is a revival.

clue.text: It's time to open cracker — revealing rubbish

indicators.note: the letters go into the middle of the other word, splitting it open

parts.note: a cracker is an attractive woman, a belle
IT as written followed by T for time, the 's acting as 'has'

explanation.surface: Pulling a Christmas cracker at the right moment and finding only junk inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracker' is not the Christmas novelty but a stunning woman, BELLE; 'to open' splits it as BEL-ITT-LE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish something is to disparage it, and so is to belittle it.

clue.text: Provide commercial vehicles on short duration

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
Minis are small cars

indicators.note: short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a term is a fixed duration

explanation.surface: Supplying advertising vans for a short period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims TERM to TER.
explanation.definitionFit: To provide or dispense something, such as medicine or justice, is a sense of this verb.

clue.text: Weird and offbeat old haunts drawing one in

indicators.note: drawing here means pulling a piece within the other one
together with drawing, it places a piece inside the jumbled letters
offbeat means unconventional, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Strange, unconventional former hangouts attracting a lone visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offbeat' rearranges OLD HAUNTS and 'drawing ... in' puts I among the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bizarre or very unusual is called strange or bizarre in this way; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Starter motor's beginning to get stiff; detach the front half

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
the first three of the six letters are cut away

parts.note: to freeze is to become stiff with cold

explanation.surface: A car engine starting to seize up in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' and 'motor' suggest an engine, but the definition is a first course. 'detach the front half' leaves EZE from FREEZE.
explanation.definitionFit: A selection of small Mediterranean dishes is often served as an appetiser.

clue.text: The setter's left with newspaperman to be introduced

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves, so 'the setter is' becomes I'M
port is the left side of a ship
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler departs with a journalist who is to be presented.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods brought in from abroad have been introduced into the country.

clue.text: Instrument's not broken, but short of odd fittings

definitions.note: the 's is 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: lacking the odd ones means the letters in odd positions are dropped and the even ones kept

explanation.surface: An instrument intact but missing a few odd parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short of odd fittings' removes the 1st, 3rd, 5th... letters of 'not broken', leaving the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-reed woodwind is a musical instrument.

clue.text: Sedatives this person consumed during manoeuvres

indicators.note: during means within, so these pieces go inside the other

parts.note: OPS is short for military operations or manoeuvres
the setter speaking of themselves is I
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: The writer took tranquillisers while on army exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcotic drugs derived from opium dull the senses and induce sleep, as sedatives do.

clue.text: Sensitive old MP I challenged near upper chamber when losing heart

indicators.note: challenged suggests being disrupted, so the letters are rearranged
losing heart means the middle letter is removed

parts.note: an attic is a room at the top of a house

explanation.surface: A veteran politician challenged near the House of Lords and losing nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upper chamber' suggests the House of Lords but is a loft room. 'challenged' rearranges OLD MP I to DIPLOM; 'when losing heart' turns ATTIC into ATIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactful and careful in delicate situations is what sensitive means here.

clue.text: Accountant perhaps — one looking for scrap?

definitions.meaning: someone who tots up, adding figures
a rag-and-bone man, collecting junk to sell, is so called in British slang

explanation.surface: A bean-counter who goes scavenging for rubbish on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, totting is collecting saleable scrap, as rag-and-bone men did with horse and cart.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is someone who adds up figures, and a scavenger of discarded goods.

clue.text: Canticle features duet with me, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A sacred song includes a duet with me, sadly.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin hymn of praise to God is a canticle sung at morning service.

clue.text: Wide-ranging — it's the same in The Odyssey maybe

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the other

parts.note: Homer's Odyssey is an example of an epic poem
idem is Latin for 'the same', used in references

explanation.surface: A claim that something sweeping is identical in Homer's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease spreading widely across a community is widespread, so the adjective covers anything wide-ranging.

clue.text: Fundamental character of book by Maxim — revolutionary

definitions.note: the fundament is the backside, and the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream is a character of that name

indicators.note: revolutionary means turned around, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a motto is a maxim, a short saying

explanation.surface: The basic nature of a book by an author, perhaps a radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns MOTTO into OTTOM. The definition puns on 'fundament', the rear, and Shakespeare's weaver.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream shares his name with the backside or fundament.

clue.text: Bank of Scotland?

parts.note: not the financial institution but a slope or hillside in Scots dialect

explanation.walkthrough: The Bank of Scotland is a famous Scottish bank; here bank means a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A hillside or steep slope by a river is called this in Scottish usage.

clue.text: Craftsman from Whitby who travels expensively?

definitions.meaning: Whitby in Yorkshire is famous for its black gemstone jewellery, so a craftsman there sets those stones
a wealthy person who flies around fashionable places

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire artisan who goes on lavish trips.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitby, a Yorkshire seaside town, is known for jewellery made of jet, a black fossil stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who mounts black gemstones, and a rich international traveller on fashionable trips.

clue.text: Muscle temperature fell

parts.note: to fell a tree is to hew it down

explanation.surface: A muscle's temperature dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' looks like the past tense of fall, but it is the verb meaning cut down.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for muscular strength, or a muscle or sinew, usually in the plural.

clue.text: Pals and welcome supporters?

definitions.meaning: humorously, a bra welcomes and supports the chest

explanation.surface: Friends who are also friendly backers.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means intimate friends, and jokingly the garments that hold up the chest.
